basis: The two submissions are byte-identical as code. I extracted both hunks and diffed them: the only differing lines are the two trailing comments. Both replace `ld a,(mkPiece)` with `ld a,(mkSide)` at the same address in the same file (movegen.inc @@ -798,8 +798,8 @@), keeping `or b`, so the promotion type in B is OR-ed with the colour bit alone instead of with the pawn's type bits. Same one-line fault localisation, same two-line change, same scope, same semantics — identical correctness_risk, minimality and clarity. Nothing process-diagnostic appears in either: neither submission carries a spec reference, an invariant/theorem name, a proof obligation, a conformance-suite or perft/self-test result, a mutation-testing note, nor a regression test — the only artefact shown is the assembly hunk itself, which is where a formal-methods process would normally leave a fingerprint (e.g. citing an encoding invariant such as "piece byte = colour | type" or the promotion clause it was checked against). The residual signals are prose style only and cut both ways, which is why I decline to guess. X's comment states the general bit-level mechanism and covers the whole failing case space ("pawn|type would set bit0: R->Q, N->B" — both reported wrong choices, i.e. reasoning over all four prompt options); Y's cites one concrete numeric instance ("1|4 would be a queen, not a rook"), which reads more like reasoning from the single reproduced test case. If forced, that asymmetry would tilt me marginally toward X as the spec-driven author, but it is a single clause of comment wording, is equally explainable as writing habit, and Y's typography (capitalised ONLY, em-dash vs X's ASCII hyphen) is an authoring-tool tell rather than a process tell. One clause of prose is not evidence a process produced a repair, so the honest answer is that the material does not distinguish them.
